questions.problem:
Compute $P(0<X<1)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}x(2-x),\, & 0\le x\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X<b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X<1) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{4}x(2-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{\int }_{0}^{1}-{x}^{2}+2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{[-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}([-\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}+(1)^{2}]-[-\frac{1}{3}(0)^{3}+(0)^{2}]) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}([-\frac{1}{3}+1]-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
P(a<X\le b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.

So, in our case, we have

$$

questions.problem:
Compute $P(X>7)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{36}x,\, & 3\le x\le 9, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a<X\le b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is identical to zero for all $x>9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>7) & ={\int }_{7}^{9}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{7}^{9}\frac{1}{36}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{72}{x}^{2}]}_{7}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{72}({9}^{2}-{7}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{72}(81-49) \\  & =\frac{32}{72} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Compute $P\left( 1 \lt   X \lt 3 \right)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14097680/assets/7059e7c4cb42e405342d34cd53ee7852f8abfffff2c3f54a95df30cdd44ef3c8.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a \lt   X \lt      b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1<X<3) & ={\int }_{1}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{18}({x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{\int }_{1}^{3}({x}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{18}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-x]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}([\frac{1}{3}(3)^{3}-(3)]-[\frac{1}{3}(1)^{3}-(1)]) \\  & =\frac{1}{18}([9-3]-[\frac{1}{3}-1]) \\  & =\frac{1}{18}(6+\frac{2}{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{18}\cdot \frac{20}{3} \\  & =\frac{10}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Compute $P\left(  X \leq 3 \right)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14097680/assets/b083c72bc5c3bb6ea1a4f5036a57e5671c884d585def9e71f17a1ac72845d984.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a \leq X \leq  b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

Since $f(x)$ is identical to zero for all $x \lt  2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & ={\int }_{2}^{3}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{2x}{45}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{45}\,{x}^{2}]}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{45}({3}^{2}-{2}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{45}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Compute $P\left( 2 \leq          X \leq          4 \right)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14097680/assets/b4da93ec01e058c31044ba7022c1e7109a7bacd4fd56c264df2ccfad5fbe2457.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a \leq        X \leq        b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

So, in our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2\le X\le 4) & ={\int }_{2}^{4}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{9}x\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{4}(x-3)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{18}{x}^{2}]}_{2}^{3}+{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}-3x]}_{3}^{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[{3}^{2}-{2}^{2}]+([\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2}-3(4)]-[\frac{1}{2}(3)^{2}-3(3)]) \\  & =\frac{5}{18}-4+\frac{9}{2} \\  & =\frac{14}{18} \\  & =\frac{7}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

The probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

This probability can be interpreted as the area bounded between $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [a,b],$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14097680/assets/e6c21e69a0dbd15ce32d18c2e74d8fcab0276e82bc55b354eaa5140adff610e6.png)

Also, remember that for continuous random variables, we get the same answer whether or not we include the endpoints of an interval $[a,b].$ In other words,

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X < b)  = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b).
$$

In this lesson, we'll get some practice at computing probabilities with continuous random variables.

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

The probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$

This probability can be interpreted as the area bounded between $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [a,b],$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14097680/assets/e6c21e69a0dbd15ce32d18c2e74d8fcab0276e82bc55b354eaa5140adff610e6.png)

Also, remember that for continuous random variables, we get the same answer whether or not we include the endpoints of an interval $[a,b].$ In other words,
